seo.title: Chapter 27 U.S. Energy Exports: Crude, LNG & Fuel Buyers
seo.shortDescription: How much crude oil, refined fuel, LNG and coal the U.S. exports, who buys it, and what each top buyer charges, from 2020–2025 UN Comtrade data.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$308.91 billion** of Chapter 27 goods in 2025, down **3.5%** from 2024. **Refined fuels (heading 2710) are 36%** of that, **crude oil (2709) 32.5%** and **natural gas, LNG and LPG (2711) 26.5%**; coal (2701) is 3.2%. The **EU takes 26%**, then Mexico (12.1%), Canada (8.7%), South Korea (5.6%) and India (4.6%). Brazil's purchases rose 31%, and China's fell **65%** to $5.1 billion.

Tariffs matter in one place. China adds 15% to U.S. coal and LNG and 10% to crude oil on top of its normal rate and its extra 10% on every U.S. good, so a U.S. LNG cargo pays about 25% and crude about 20%, and the announcement says the energy tariffs cannot be waived. Crude oil, LNG and coal enter the EU duty-free, and Mexico and Canada charge nothing under USMCA. For most buyers, what decides sales is price, freight and long-term contracts, and the U.S. side is a licensing question for LNG, not a tariff.

keyTakeaways: Three products are about 94% of this chapter: refined fuels (2710) 36%, crude oil (2709) 32.5% and natural gas and LNG (2711) 26.5%. Coal is 3.2%.
The EU (26.3%), Mexico (12.1%) and Canada (8.7%) take 47%. Crude oil, LNG and coal enter the EU duty-free, and Mexico and Canada charge nothing under USMCA.
China is the one buyer that taxes U.S. energy heavily, about 20% on crude, 25% on LNG and 28–31% on coal once its added tariffs stack, and its purchases fell 65% in 2025.

The U.S. side is routine for crude oil and coal, but LNG needs Department of Energy authorization (automatic for free-trade-agreement countries), and sanctions bar sales to Cuba, Iran and other embargoed destinations.
